strengths: Well-motivated problem analysis with clear empirical evidence of root causes (semantic mask overlap) leading to count failures and semantic mixing
Practical training-free and model-agnostic approach that generalizes across multiple diffusion model architectures (SD1.4, SD1.5, SD3.5-M, SDXL) without fine-tuning
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks showing consistent improvements (1.9× over baseline, 56%→83% multi-instance accuracy on IntraCompBench)
Introduction of IntraCompBench, a well-designed benchmark addressing a gap in existing evaluation suites by focusing on intra-category multi-object compositions
Thorough experimental rigor with detailed ablation studies, sensitivity analyses, and multiple baselines demonstrating scientific quality
Clear technical presentation with intuitive two-phase design (Instance Formation + Instance-aware Semantic Separation) supported by effective visualizations
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: combines existing techniques (self-attention clustering, MPO loss, repel-and-bind loss) without introducing fundamentally new concepts
Substantial computational overhead (~10× latency increase, e.g., 10.7s→111.4s for SDXL) severely restricts practical deployment for interactive or real-time applications, undermining practical claims
Critical unresolved limitation: acknowledged failure on 3D spatial reasoning scenarios (objects behind transparent materials, depth-based positioning) with no clear extension path
Significant external dependency on LLM-based prompt parsing (10 seconds latency, 40GB VRAM) that fails on ambiguous count expressions, reducing claim of being truly 'training-free'
Evaluation limited to 2-5 objects; scalability to complex multi-object scenes (>5 objects) and cross-category scenarios remains unclear
Hyperparameter sensitivity (step size η, loss schedule) requires careful tuning but limited guidance provided for practitioners on selection strategy
IntraCompBench built from COCO dataset biases; design focused on intra-category mixing may not reflect performance on diverse cross-category scenarios

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real failure modes in multi-object text-to-image generation with clear empirical demonstration (count failures and semantic mixing)
Elegant two-phase hierarchical design leveraging self-attention structure for instance formation followed by semantic refinement—grounded in understanding of diffusion dynamics
Training-free approach makes method generally applicable across different diffusion models without model retraining
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three benchmarks with consistent improvements and detailed ablations (Tables 2-6 show ~6-8% gains)
Valuable new benchmark (IntraCompBench) that specifically isolates intra-category multi-object compositions where failures are most severe, addressing a gap in existing evaluation
Extensive supplementary analysis including clustering algorithm comparisons, fine-tuned model integration, stability analysis across seeds, and application to layout-to-image generation
Clear visual improvements demonstrated in qualitative results (Figures 5, 18-20) across diverse prompts and object combinations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily orchestrates existing components (self-attention analysis, attention-based guidance, repel-and-bind losses) hierarchically; incremental rather than groundbreaking contribution

Significant computational overhead inadequately addressed: 2-3× latency increase (10s→30s+) and substantial VRAM overhead (30+ GB) largely confined to appendix; may severely limit practical deployment despite being training-free

Critical LLM dependency undermines 'training-free' claim: method requires external LLM-based prompt parsing (GPT-OSS) to extract class tokens, counts, and relations; introduces external failure mode and circular dependency not clearly disclosed upfront

Weak theoretical justification for core assumptions: why self-attention early in diffusion reliably encodes instance boundaries lacks rigorous analysis; only empirical evidence provided; background gate assumptions (Eq. 3-5) not validated across diverse scene types

Narrow evaluation scope: IntraCompBench limited to 4 COCO supercategories with 2-5 objects only; 3D spatial reasoning explicitly out of scope; generalization to complex scenes with 6+ objects or diverse categories unexplored

Loss schedule design appears ad-hoc with limited justification: linear weighting λ_ins(t)=t/T significantly outperforms alternatives (Table 5) but no principled derivation provided; suggests method requires careful tuning

High sensitivity to hyperparameters and design choices: step size η requires trade-off tuning (Figure 8), metric choice (MPO vs KL) substantially impacts results (36% vs 15% gain in Table 6), loss schedule critical—robustness across diverse scenarios unclear

Limited generalization evaluation: primarily SDXL-focused; minimal assessment on other recent models (brief Flux mention); no evaluation on older models or systematic comparison of effectiveness across model architectures

Incomplete baseline comparisons: recent methods undertreated (TokenCompose, IterComp only in appendix); Bounded Attention dismissed from one failure case; some baselines from 2021-2022; comparison with supervised methods (Table 3) conflates LLM parsing as 'training-free'

Failure modes underexplored: only Figure 15 shows 3D spatial limitation; systematic analysis of when clustering fails, instance identification degrades, or method underperforms missing; no quantification of impact from prompt parsing errors
Modest aesthetic quality gains: FID/CMMD improvements in Table 13 are marginal (~2%), suggesting method primarily affects composition without substantially improving visual quality

Reproducibility concerns: code availability unconfirmed; LLM parsing dependency and multiple hyperparameters may hinder exact reproduction; no systematic analysis of clustering stability (random initialization)

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear analysis of failure modes (Figures 1-3) showing semantic overlap in attention maps correlates with mixing failures
Novel application of hierarchical instance-first attention control, combining self-attention clustering with instance-aware cross-attention masking in an intuitive two-phase framework
Practical training-free approach with significant advantage over methods requiring fine-tuning, enabling broad applicability and reproducibility

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (T2I-CompBench, HRS-Bench, IntraCompBench) with extensive ablations on loss schedules, clustering algorithms, normalization, and hyperparameter sensitivity
Strong empirical results showing 1.9× improvements on multi-instance accuracy and 70-76% counting accuracy without supervised labels, consistently outperforming existing methods
Valuable new benchmark (IntraCompBench) addressing genuine gap by isolating intra-category multi-object failures which are particularly challenging and common
Demonstrated generalization to layout-to-image controllers and fine-tuned models (Table 12), showing complementarity and flexibility
Excellent presentation quality with effective figures, clear writing, thorough implementation details, and promised code release supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—combines well-established techniques (self-attention/cross-attention manipulation, K-means clustering, MPO metrics) in a new application rather than introducing fundamental innovations

Significant computational overhead not fully addressed: 2-3× latency increase for large models (Table 14), substantial VRAM overhead, and expensive K-means clustering at each denoising step with limited efficiency-accuracy discussion

Fundamental 3D spatial understanding limitation (acknowledged in Section C.5, Figure 15) with no clear path forward; method captures only 2D occupancy, failing on transparent objects and depth-related scenarios
Hyperparameter choices appear somewhat ad-hoc: η=0.01 for gradient steps and β=100 for normalization chosen empirically with limited sensitivity analysis and insufficient justification

Incomplete handling of ambiguous linguistic quantifiers ('a few', 'several') where LLM parser fails, affecting real-world prompt robustness though workaround of sampling small candidate sets is pragmatic

Limited error analysis and failure case investigation—IntraCompBench evaluates but doesn't deeply analyze when/why the method fails, sensitivity to object semantic similarity, or performance with extreme aspect ratios
Clustering procedure in Phase 1 involves multiple heuristic steps with underjustified choice of K-means; sensitivity to these choices and assumption of clear SA separations not fully explored
Missing analysis of scalability to very dense multi-object scenes (>10 instances) and evaluation of robustness to object size variations and crowded scenarios

Incomplete comparison scope: OverLayBench excluded due to data format issues, limited comparison with other training-free semantic control approaches, and CountGen analysis lacks deep investigation of improvement sources
